title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Oral melanoacanthoma is a rare, benign lesion of the oral mucosa that often appears clinically suspicious for malignancy. The presentation can vary in color, size, and location, commonly involving sites such as the buccal mucosa. Due to its appearance, which resembles that of more concerning pigmented lesions, a definitive diagnosis requires histopathological examination. The proliferation of dendritic melanocytes and keratinocytes characterizes the condition. Although oral melanoacanthoma is benign, its rapid growth and pigmentation may raise concern for malignancy. This activity examines the clinical features and diagnostic workup for oral melanoacanthoma and emphasizes the importance of distinguishing it from other pigmented oral lesions to ensure appropriate management.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Continuing Education Activity
content: By completing this educational activity, learners strengthen their ability to identify the varied manifestations of oral melanoacanthoma and appreciate the indispensable role of tissue diagnosis. The program highlights the value of coordinated care involving dentists, oral pathologists, dermatologists, and laboratory professionals to optimize the diagnostic process and guide management. Integrating insights from multiple disciplines promotes timely recognition, reduces unnecessary procedures, and provides adequate patient reassurance when indicated. This collaborative, patient-centered approach supports high-quality care grounded in accurate, evidence-based assessment.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Introduction
content: Oral melanoacanthoma is a rare, benign oral lesion that usually presents as a rapidly growing, asymptomatic brown-black macule. The lesion typically develops secondary to tissue trauma; in the literature, up to 75% of reported cases are labeled as reactive. [1] Histologically, the biopsy demonstrates acanthosis of the superficial epithelium and proliferation of dendritic melanocytes. [2]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Introduction
content: The most common site of oral melanoacanthomas is the buccal mucosa, but the lesion can also occur on the labial mucosa, palate, gingiva, alveolar mucosa, and oropharynx. [1] There are 2 recognized phenotypes: singular and multifocal, the former being the most common. Oral melanoacanthoma is self-limiting; once diagnosed, further intervention is generally not indicated.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Etiology
content: The etiology of oral melanoacanthoma remains undetermined, but it is most often associated with trauma to the oral mucosa, which stimulates melanocyte activity; a review of 56 articles on 115 cases concluded that 75% of authors reported a reactive etiology. [1] [3] This theory is corroborated by the reactive eosinophilic infiltrate observed on histopathology. Chronic trauma or chemical irritants stimulate melanocytes, leading to the oral pigmentation characteristic of melanoacanthoma.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Etiology
content: Regular contact with petroleum-derived ingredients in toothpaste and mouthwash may also irritate. These derivatives include sodium lauryl sulfate, phenolphthalein, nitrophenol, chlorophenol, phenylenediamine sulfate, amine fluoride, and cocamidopropyl betaine. Hydrogen peroxide mouthwashes can also irritate the oral mucosa and cause melanoacanthoma.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Etiology
content: Silver amalgam has been described as a causative agent that may induce morphologic changes and pigmentation, as well as dental restorations with other materials. [1] Bruxism, poorly fitted removable prostheses, biting of the cheeks, implant surgery, and nonspecific chronic trauma have been reported features preceding the presentation of oral melanoacanthoma. Other etiologic associations include chronic asthma treatment and chronic use of ferrous lactate for iron-deficiency anemia.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Epidemiology
content: Oral melanoacanthoma may occur at any stage in adult life, but it is predominantly encountered in the younger age group, with a median age at diagnosis of 35. The condition has a female predilection, with a 3:2 female-to-male ratio. Oral melanoacanthoma is most frequently observed in Black individuals, although cases have also been reported in White and Hispanic or Latino individuals. [1] [2] Solitary lesions are more frequently observed in the buccal mucosa, while the multifocal subtype tends to occur mostly on the palate. [4]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Pathophysiology
content: Oral melanoacanthoma is a rare, benign, pigmented lesion of the oral mucosa characterized by a reactive, rather than neoplastic, pathophysiology. The lesion is characterized by its sudden onset and rapid growth, often in areas subject to chronic irritation or trauma, such as the buccal mucosa, gingiva, or palate. [5]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Histopathology
content: A biopsy is mandatory for the diagnosis of oral melanoacanthoma. Histopathologically, oral melanoacanthoma shows acanthosis (thickening) of the epithelium and proliferation of melanin-producing dendritic cells (melanocytes) distributed throughout all epithelial layers, not just the basal layer. [6] [7] [8] These melanocytes are often immunoreactive for markers such as human melanoma black 45 (HMB-45) and S-100 protein, confirming their melanocytic origin. The presence of increased melanophages in the underlying connective tissue is also common. [9]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- History and Physical
content: Oral melanoacanthoma typically presents as a new, well-circumscribed, pigmented lesion in the mouth which is generally brown or black in color. The lesion may be flat or raised. Almost half of the cases of melanoacanthoma are located on the buccal mucosa, followed by the palate and lips, and, less commonly, the gums. [1] [4] [10] The palate is more commonly affected by the multifocal subtype. Multifocal lesions are usually darker and smaller in diameter, and they typically occur in groups of 2 to 5. [4] In rare instances, patients may present with diffuse oral pigmentation. [11] Because the lesions exhibit rapid radial growth, oral melanoacanthoma can often be mistaken for melanoma; oral melanomas most commonly affect the hard palate.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- History and Physical
content: Oral melanoacanthomas are usually asymptomatic, but they may be painful or itchy. History-taking generally elicits classic risk factors such as bruxism, aggressive brushing, recent dental procedures, oral trauma, or, most commonly, a new mouthwash, toothpaste, or teeth-whitening agent. A family history of pigmented oral lesions or polyposis may suggest Peutz-Jegher syndrome. A thorough oral exam to assess for additional lesions should be performed, as well as a full skin exam to assess for concomitant nevi or suspicious melanocytic lesions. Oral melanoacanthomas tend to regress spontaneously, but the lesions may exhibit rapid growth before stabilization and regression.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Evaluation
content: Since oral melanoacanthomas lack distinctive clinical features compared to melanoma, diagnosis is based on histopathological findings. Immunohistochemical staining with monoclonal antibodies against S-100 and HMB-45 is a useful tool for confirming the presence of melanocyte dendritic cells. [9] [12]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Treatment / Management
content: Oral melanoacanthoma is a benign entity with no known risk of malignant transformation; once diagnosed, further treatment is not necessary. [13] Clinical regression of the lesion is observed even immediately after a high-frequency incisional biopsy. If treatment is desired, the lesion may be surgically excised with negative margins. Argon plasma coagulation has also been used with promising results. [14]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Treatment / Management
content: Cryotherapy, curettage, and topical fluorouracil 5% are other treatment options described in the literature. The recurrence of oral melanoacanthoma after treatment is exceedingly rare, and the prognosis remains excellent. Routine follow-up is recommended to ensure diagnostic accuracy, but further intervention is generally unnecessary.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of pigmented oral lesions spans from benign entities to rare but aggressive conditions such as oral melanoma. Melanocytic lesions can be classified as either solitary or multifocal. [15] Oral melanoacanthoma typically presents as a solitary lesion, although in rare cases it may be multifocal or diffuse. The following list categorizes pigmented oral lesions in the differential diagnosis of oral melanoacanthoma.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Focal melanocytic lesions most commonly present as melanocytic macules, followed by melanocytic nevi; oral melanoma is rare but clinically significant. Oral melanoma should be suspected when lesions exhibit ABCDE warning signs: A symmetry, B order irregularity, variation in C olor, D iameter greater than 6 mm, and E levation, or when the lesion is raised. Oral melanoma accounts for nearly 25% of head and neck melanomas and carries a poor prognosis, with an approximate 30% 5-year survival rate due to its aggressive metastatic potential and high recurrence risk. Although rare, its severity warrants a prompt biopsy to exclude the diagnosis. [16] [17]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Multifocal melanocytic lesions may include smoker’s melanosis, which occurs in individuals who smoke or chew tobacco. Other causes of multifocal hyperpigmentation include systemic conditions such as HIV infection, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, neurofibromatosis, McCune-Albright syndrome, primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), and Laugier-Hunziker syndrome, as well as drug-induced pigmentation from agents such as azathioprine, antimalarials, cytotoxic drugs (eg, bleomycin), and oral contraceptives. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may cause melanocytic oral hyperpigmentation in up to 18% of patients with HIV, most frequently on the gingival mucosa, independent of antiretroviral therapy, CD4 count, or disease duration. [18] Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by benign hyperpigmented buccal macules and gastrointestinal hamartomas or polyposis. The condition is linked to increased risk of cancers, including those of the stomach, colon, and pancreas. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome often presents in childhood with oral and cutaneous macules affecting the lips, oral mucosa, and perioral skin. Patients with oral/perioral pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyps, or with a family history suggestive of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, should undergo genetic testing. [19] [20] Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) causes oral mucosal hyperpigmentation through increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone secondary to the pathologically elevated adrenocorticotropic levels. Laugier-Hunziker syndrome is a rare, benign cause of oral and cutaneous hyperpigmentation, typically affecting older White men, without associated hamartomas or malignancy; it is a diagnosis of exclusion. [21] [22]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Nonmelanocytic diffuse oral pigmentation may result from heavy metal exposure, trauma, or systemic iron overload (hemochromatosis).

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Amalgam tattoos (focal argyria) are blue or gray discolorations of the oral mucosa adjacent to prior dental work such as fillings, implants, or prostheses. These lesions may be radiographically visible, and histologically, they reveal fine black deposits along collagen fibers and blood vessels. If the history does not support a benign, non-melanocytic cause, a biopsy is warranted. [23]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Physiologic (racial) oral pigmentation is common in darker-skinned individuals and typically presents as symmetric, diffuse brown-black macules, often on the gingiva or buccal mucosa. The macules are stable, asymptomatic, and lack a history of trauma or rapid growth. Dermatoscopy typically shows a homogeneous pattern. [24]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for oral melanoacanthoma is excellent. The condition has been shown to spontaneously regress or resolve after the biopsy procedure or cessation of offending agents. [3] Oral melanoacanthoma lesions can be present for periods of weeks up to a year and may exhibit growth or progression before patients seek medical treatment. [4] In some cases, a solitary lesion may progress to multiple lesions or diffuse pigmentation. [13] There are no reported cases of progression to atypia, dysplasia, or malignancy. [25]

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Complications
content: There are no reported complications from oral melanoacanthoma itself. Complications associated with the diagnosis are mostly secondary to surgical excisions, such as scarring and post-operative pain. Electing to not biopsy a pigmented oral lesion may lead to a missed malignancy diagnosis, so it is prudent for the oral surgeon to biopsy all pigmented lesions unless there is a clear component of the patient's history that indicates a benign etiology.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients should be educated about the potential association between offending agents or dental implants and oral melanoacanthoma. Gleaning information from patients about the use of off-label dental agents or implants is an essential part of history-taking. In many cases, the lesion resolves with cessation of the offending agent. [4] Despite oral melanoacanthoma being a benign lesion, it is critical to educate patients about the similarity it has in appearance to oral melanoma and to emphasize the necessity of a biopsy.

title: Oral Melanoacanthoma -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Enhancing awareness among dentists, oral surgeons, and primary care clinicians regarding the benign, reactive nature of oral melanoacanthoma is vital for accurate diagnosis and effective patient counseling. Improved understanding reduces unnecessary alarm when a new pigmented lesion is identified, particularly when a local irritant or triggering factor is present. Because these lesions may first be detected in the primary care setting, timely referral to a dental professional for histopathologic confirmation remains essential, as clinical examination alone cannot establish the diagnosis. Although no active treatment is typically required, elimination of contributing irritants and planned clinical monitoring support resolution. Thorough patient education is also essential; individuals should be encouraged to report new or changing areas of oral pigmentation and to attend coordinated follow-up evaluations until complete regression is documented.
